finding: The live range of $200-$825 is about right at the bottom and too low at the top. Built totals for one front CV axle, parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr (the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2013 Honda Fit automatic about $217-$1,282 (1.1-1.6 hr); midsize 2016 Jeep Cherokee 3.2L about $235-$823 (0.5-1.6 hr); truck 2019 Silverado 1500 4WD about $255-$918 (1.0-2.4 hr); luxury 2015 Acura ILX 2.4L about $210-$710 (1.0-1.6 hr). Nothing is left null. The bottom: the lowest totals ($210-$255) pair a new aftermarket axle at an online price ($85-$175) with a manufacturer warranty time or a seller's one-hour figure, so $200 is a fair floor and few real quotes will come in under it. The top: $825 covers an aftermarket axle on every class and a dealer-list axle on the Cherokee and the ILX 2.4L, but not the cars whose genuine shafts are expensive. Honda lists the Fit's shaft at $1,026-$1,057, which builds to about $1,280; it lists the 2015 Accord's at $1,084-$1,116 (about $1,340 built), and Acura lists the ILX 2.0L shaft at $1,346-$1,432 (about $1,480-$1,610 with 1.1 hr). RepairPal's national average ($1,283-$1,381, with $1,075 in parts) and J.D. Power's $1,500 top figure sit in the same place. A ceiling of about $1,350 would cover a dealer-parts job on a mainstream car; $825 fits only if the range is meant to describe aftermarket parts. The spread is almost entirely parts: labor is only about $60-$385 in every class. How solid the labor times are: three classes now have a manufacturer time for the example vehicle. Economy: Honda's recall warranty time for the Fit itself, 1.1 hr for the right side (1.5 hr for the left on an automatic), including inspection, wheel alignment and test drive. Midsize: FCA's recall time for the 2016 Cherokee 3.2L left halfshaft, 0.5 hr, which is unusually short (a new vehicle, no alignment) and is backed by a seller's 'approximately 1 hour' for the same vehicle; treat the bottom of that class as optimistic. The aftermarket Cherokee axle's page does not state the engine, so its fit on the 3.2L is not confirmed. Truck: a parts seller's 'approx 1 hour' for the Silverado itself, with GM's 2.4 hr warranty time for both sides on the same truck used as a ceiling because no one-side time was printed; a seller quotes about 3 hours for the previous-generation truck. Second look at trucks (2026-11-20), no change to the numbers: FCA's recall S32 allows 0.8 hr to replace BOTH front halfshafts on a 2016 Ram 1500 4WD (nearly new trucks, no alignment), and an FCA bulletin allows 0.5 hr for one side on a 2025 Ram 1500 RHO without saying clearly what that covers. Both are kept as cross-checks only. They are for a different truck, the first is a both-sides time and the second is unclear, and switching the example to the Ram would have cut the truck's labor to under 0.8 hr on the strength of new-vehicle warranty allowances that sit far below GM's 2.4 hr for both sides of a Silverado. What they do show is that makers disagree widely on this job for pickups, so the truck's 1.0-2.4 hr is a loose bracket, not a measured one, and a one-side manufacturer time for the Silverado is still missing. Luxury is unchanged and the weakest: the Acura time is for the ILX with the other powertrain, not the 2.4L manual car, and no aftermarket axle with a price was found for the powertrain the bulletin covers. Acura's 1.2 hr for one front driveshaft on a 2021 RDX, alignment included, sits inside the luxury range. The 1.6 hr high end in the economy, midsize and luxury classes is one flat-rate figure quoted by an independent mechanic for a 2015 Subaru Forester, from a guide he does not name; GM's 1.1 hr for a Cruze right half shaft and Honda's 1.0-1.1 hr for a Civic Hybrid sit inside the range. Because half of the eight hour figures are still not for the example vehicle, confidence stays low. Warranty times are the low end of what shops bill, J.D. Power's general statement is 1.5 to 3 hours, and a seized axle nut or a shaft rusted into the hub adds time.
extras: A quote often adds a new axle nut (usually one-time-use), an axle seal at the transmission or front differential if it is leaking or disturbed, and a top-up of transmission fluid or gear oil lost when the shaft comes out (the Honda bulletins include a fluid check). Some shops add a wheel alignment, though the manufacturer times above already include one. Shops may recommend the other side at the same time, which roughly doubles parts and adds less than double the labor (Honda allows 1.4-1.9 hr for both against 1.0-1.5 hr for one). Also possible: a refundable core charge on a remanufactured axle, the separate intermediate shaft or its bearing on cars that have one, extra labor for a seized axle nut or a shaft rusted into the wheel hub (sometimes a new wheel bearing as a result), a diagnosis or inspection fee, shop supplies and sales tax.
